subject: maths
title: Chapter 8 · Test 4
summary: Chapter test 4 for Year 7 Statistics and probability: data types, graphs, averages and range, probability and relative frequency.
body:
Chapter 8 · Test 4 checks everything from Chapter 8 — Statistics and probability: collecting and classifying data, displaying data in graphs and plots, the mean, median, mode and range, chance and the probability scale, and experiments with relative frequency.

## How to do this test

- **Time:** about 25 minutes for 15 multiple-choice questions.
- **Conditions:** no notes, and no calculator unless the question says. Work on paper.
- **Levels:** 4 Easy, 5 Medium, 4 Hard and 2 Challenge questions.
- **Afterwards:** for any question you got wrong, go back to the lesson named in its topic and try the practice questions again.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a statistical question?

options.A: How many hours do Year 7 students sleep on a school night?
options.B: What are the favourite sports of students in my class?
options.C: How tall are the players in my basketball club?
options.D: How many brothers do I have?

questions.explanation: A statistical question is answered by collecting data that varies. "How many brothers do I have?" has only one answer, so it is not statistical.
steps: Step 1: a statistical question needs data from many people or things, with answers that vary.
Step 2: the questions about Year 7 students, your class and your club all collect varying data.
Step 3: "How many brothers do I have?" has just one answer, so it is not statistical.

mistakes.A: Step 2: this asks about many students whose answers vary, so it is statistical.
mistakes.B: Step 2: different students give different answers, so it is statistical.
mistakes.C: Step 2: each player has a different height, so the answers vary — it is statistical.

questions.prompt: Which of these is categorical data, even though it is written with numbers?

options.A: The numbers on footy players' jumpers
options.B: The number of goals each player kicked

questions.explanation: Jumper numbers are labels that name a player — an average jumper number means nothing — so they are categorical. Goals, heights and ages are all real amounts.
steps: Step 1: ask "would an average of these make sense?"
Step 2: an average of goals, heights or ages makes sense, so those are numerical.
Step 3: an average jumper number means nothing — jumper numbers are labels, so they are categorical.

mistakes.B: Step 2: goals are counted and an average makes sense, so this is numerical discrete data.
mistakes.C: Step 2: heights are measured and an average makes sense, so this is numerical continuous data.
mistakes.D: Step 2: age is measured time and an average makes sense, so this is numerical.

questions.prompt: 25 students were asked how many times they visited the library this term. The frequency table shows: 0 times → 6, 1 time → 8, 2 times → 5, 3 times → 4, 4 times → 2. What percentage of the students visited at least twice?
questions.explanation: "At least twice" means 2, 3 or 4 visits: 5 + 4 + 2 = 11 students. 11/25 = 44/100 = 44%.
steps: Step 1: "at least twice" means 2, 3 or 4 times: 5 + 4 + 2 = 11 students.
Step 2: as a fraction of all 25 students: 11/25.

mistakes.A: Step 1: "at least twice" means 2, 3 or 4 times — you only counted 2 times.
mistakes.C: Step 1: "at least twice" doesn't include students who visited once.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 11 is the number of students. Change 11 out of 25 into a percentage.

questions.prompt: The heights of seven seedlings (in cm) are 12, 14, 13, 15, 14, 38, 13. On a dot plot, which value is an outlier?
questions.explanation: Most heights cluster between 12 and 15 cm, but 38 cm is far away from the rest, so it is an outlier.
steps: Step 1: look at where the values cluster: 12, 13, 13, 14, 14, 15 are all close together.
Step 2: 38 is far from the rest of the data, so it is the outlier.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 12 is the smallest value, but it is close to the others. An outlier is far away from the rest.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 14 is a common value in the middle of the cluster, not an outlier.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 26 is the range (38 − 12). An outlier is one of the data values.

questions.prompt: 40 students were asked how they get to school, and 14 said they walk. What angle should the "walk" sector have in a pie chart?
questions.explanation: Each student is worth 360° ÷ 40 = 9°, so 14 students need 14 × 9° = 126°. 35° confuses the percentage (35%) with the angle.
steps: Step 1: the walk sector is 14 out of 40 students, so it is 14/40 of the circle.
Step 2: each student is worth 360° ÷ 40 = 9°.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the frequency isn't the angle — 14 students is not 14°. Find 14/40 of 360°.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 14/40 = 35% — that is a percentage. Multiply the fraction by 360°, not 100.
mistakes.C: Step 2: a full circle is 360°, not 180°.

questions.prompt: A stem-and-leaf plot (key: 4 | 7 means 47) shows: stem 3 → leaves 2 5 8; stem 4 → leaves 0 1 4 6 9; stem 5 → leaves 3 7. What is the median?
questions.explanation: There are 10 values, so the median is halfway between the 5th and 6th values: 41 and 44. (41 + 44) ÷ 2 = 42.5.
steps: Step 1: count the leaves: 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 values, already in order: 32, 35, 38, 40, 41, 44, 46, 49, 53, 57.
Step 2: 10 is even, so the two middle values are the 5th and 6th: 41 and 44.

mistakes.B: Step 2: with 10 values there are two middle values — find halfway between them, not just the first.
mistakes.C: Step 2: with 10 values there are two middle values — find halfway between them, not just the second.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the median is the middle of the ordered values, not halfway between the smallest and largest.

questions.explanation: Range = largest − smallest = 31 − 12 = 19. Adding them gives 43, which is wrong.
steps: Step 1: the largest value is 31 and the smallest is 12.
Step 2: range = 31 − 12 = 19.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you subtracted the last value from the first. Find the largest and smallest values first.
mistakes.C: Step 2: subtract the smallest from the largest — don't add them.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 23 is the median (the middle). The range is largest minus smallest.

questions.prompt: In a survey of favourite colours, blue got 7 votes, red 9, green 4 and yellow 9. What is the mode?
questions.explanation: Red and yellow both have the highest frequency (9), so the data is bimodal: the modes are red and yellow. 9 is their frequency, not the mode.
steps: Step 1: the mode is the category with the highest frequency.
Step 2: the highest frequency is 9, shared by red and yellow — so there are two modes: red and yellow.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 9 is how many votes the top colours got. The mode is the category itself.
mistakes.B: Step 2: yellow also got 9 votes — when two categories tie for the most, both are modes.
mistakes.D: Step 2: there is no mode only when every value has the same frequency. Here two colours are ahead.

questions.prompt: Three whole numbers have a mean of 12 and a median of 10. The smallest number is 6. What is the largest number?
questions.explanation: The total is 12 × 3 = 36. The numbers are 6, 10 (the median) and the largest, so the largest = 36 − 6 − 10 = 20.
steps: Step 1: total of the three numbers = mean × 3 = 12 × 3 = 36.
Step 2: the numbers in order are 6, 10 (the median), and the largest.

mistakes.A: Step 2: subtract both known numbers from the total — you forgot to subtract the 6.
mistakes.B: Step 2: subtract both known numbers from the total — you forgot to subtract the median, 10.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the mean is not halfway between the smallest and largest numbers. Find the total first: mean × 3.

questions.prompt: Which probability describes an event that is likely?
questions.explanation: Likely events have a probability between ½ and 1. 0.8 is in that range, so it is likely. 0.2 is below ½, so it is unlikely.
steps: Step 1: on the probability scale, likely means between ½ (0.5) and 1.
Step 2: only 0.8 is between 0.5 and 1, so 0.8 is likely.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 0.2 is less than ½, so the event is unlikely.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 0.5 is exactly ½, which is an even chance.

questions.prompt: A bag holds 6 red, 2 blue and 4 white balls. One ball is picked at random. What is the probability that it is NOT white?
questions.explanation: There are 12 balls and 8 are not white (6 red + 2 blue), so P(not white) = 8/12 = 2/3. Or: 1 − 4/12 = 2/3.
steps: Step 1: total = 6 + 2 + 4 = 12 balls.
Step 2: not white = red or blue: 6 + 2 = 8 balls, so P = 8/12.
Step 3: simplify: 8/12 = 2/3.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 4/12 = 1/3 is the chance of white. You need NOT white.
mistakes.C: Step 2: "not white" means red or blue — you only counted the red balls.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the bottom number is ALL 12 balls, not just the white ones. A probability can't be more than 1.

questions.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed at the same time. What is the probability of getting two heads?
questions.explanation: The equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. Only HH gives two heads, so P = 1/4. Thinking there are 3 results (HH, one of each, TT) gives 1/3, but "one of each" can happen in two ways.
steps: Step 1: list the sample space: HH, HT, TH, TT — 4 equally likely outcomes.
Step 2: only HH is two heads, so P(two heads) = 1/4.

mistakes.A: Step 1: there are four equally likely outcomes, not three — HT and TH are different results.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 1/2 is the chance for one coin. With two coins, list all the outcomes.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 3/4 is the chance of NOT getting two heads.

questions.prompt: A fair spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5. It is spun 150 times. About how many times would you expect it to land on 5?
questions.explanation: P(5) = 1/5, so expected number = 1/5 × 150 = 30. Using 1/6 (as for a die) gives 25, but this spinner has 5 sections.
steps: Step 1: the theoretical probability of landing on 5 is 1/5.
Step 2: expected number = probability × number of spins = 1/5 × 150 = 30.

mistakes.A: Step 2: multiply the probability (1/5) by 150 — don't multiply 150 by 5.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the spinner has 5 sections, not 6 like a die, so P(5) = 1/5.
mistakes.C: Step 2: don't subtract. Expected number = probability × number of spins.

questions.prompt: Hayley tosses a bottle cap 40 times and it lands on its side 12 times. Raj tosses the same cap 200 times and it lands on its side 45 times. Whose result gives the better estimate of the probability of landing on its side, and what is that estimate?
questions.explanation: Raj did many more trials, so his estimate is more trustworthy: 45 ÷ 200 = 0.225. Hayley's 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3 comes from only 40 tosses.
steps: Step 1: more trials give a better estimate, so use Raj's 200 tosses.
Step 2: Raj's relative frequency = 45 ÷ 200 = 0.225.

mistakes.B: Step 1: more trials give a better estimate — Raj did 200 tosses, Hayley only 40.
mistakes.C: Step 2: divide 45 by Raj's 200 tosses, not by 100.
mistakes.D: Step 1: more trials give a better estimate — and 12 must be divided by 40.

questions.prompt: A spinner is split into a red half, a blue quarter and a green quarter. It is spun 80 times. About how many times would you expect it to land on blue?
questions.explanation: Blue is a quarter of the spinner, so P(blue) = 1/4 and the expected number is 1/4 × 80 = 20. Treating the three colours as equally likely (80 ÷ 3 ≈ 27) is wrong because the sections are different sizes.
steps: Step 1: blue takes up a quarter of the spinner, so P(blue) = 1/4 (the colours are not equally likely).
Step 2: expected number = 1/4 × 80 = 20.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the three colours are not equally likely — blue is only a quarter of the spinner, not a third.
mistakes.C: Step 1: red is the half. Blue is a quarter of the spinner.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 60 is how many times you would expect it NOT to land on blue.
